To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IL-1 and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) increase the secretory response to a hypothalamic releasing factor (CRF) by stimulating the release of CRF from hypothalamic neurons, and that this is mediated by a mechanism involving the activation of the hypothalaminic CRF neuron by the neurotransmitter glutamate.

the cytokines IL-1beta, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma increase ACTH and corticosterone release from the HPA, and that these actions are mediated by the hypothalamus and involve activation of hypothalamic CRH neurons.

the HPA axis is activated by numerous members of several families of cytokines, including IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, IL-11, IL-12, IL-15, interferon-alpha, interferon-gamma, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor, and granulocyte colony stimulating factor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which cytokine signals are transmitted to the neuroendocrine brain.
the mechanisms by which the immune system signals the neuroendocrine system and how this bidirectional communication influences the function and development of the immune system.
the neuroendocrine-immune interface, which is the site of a bidirectional communication between these two systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HPA axis is a major target for the action of cytokines.
the HPA axis is a major target of the cytokine system, and that the neuroendocrine effects of cytokines are mediated by the activation of the HPA system.
the regulation of the HPA by cytokines is a complex process that involves multiple cytokines, multiple neuroanatomic pathways, and multiple mechanisms of action.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cytokines are potent activators of HPA axis activity and that this neuroendocrine activity is a fundamental mechanism by which the immune system communicates with the brain.
the cytokine-induced activation of the HPA is a highly complex process, involving the participation of numerous cytokines, acting at multiple sites, through multiple mechanisms.

the neuroendocrine actions of cytokines are mediated by a complex network of interactions involving the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, the median eminence, the pituitary gland, the adrenal gland, and the hippocampus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cytokines are potent regulators of HPA axis hormone production, and the mechanisms of cytokine action are likely to be relevant to understanding the pathophysiological consequences of chronic cytokine exposure.
the HPA axis can be activated by a variety of cytokines, which can act at the level of both the brain and the periphery, to produce a coordinated response that is designed to maintain homeostasis.

cytokines have a profound impact upon neuroendocrine function, and that the mechanisms by which cytokine signals are transduced to the neuroendocrine axis are likely to be complex and involve both classical neuroendocrine and immune mechanisms.
